notes.meaning: The angel of the Lord traveled from Gilgal to Bochim to deliver a divine message to Israel. He reminded the people that He had brought them out of Egypt into the promised land and had sworn never to break His covenant with them. Traditional commentators understand this angel to be the Lord Himself appearing in visible form before His coming in Christ.

God reminded the Israelites of His clear command to avoid making treaties with the wicked inhabitants of Canaan and to tear down their pagan altars. Instead of obeying, the people compromised and let the altars remain. The Lord asked them why they had disobeyed, showing that there was no good excuse for their actions.

Because the people refused to obey, God withdrew His promise to drive out the Canaanites before them. The remaining pagan nations would now trouble Israel like sharp thorns in their sides. Their false gods would become a deadly trap, luring the Israelites into spiritual ruin.

When the angel finished speaking these piercing words, the entire assembly was overcome with sorrow. The people broke into loud weeping as they realized the painful consequences of their disobedience. Yet their tears were only a temporary burst of emotion and did not lead to a lasting change of heart.

The people named the gathering place Bochim, which means 'weepers,' because of their loud crying. They also offered animal sacrifices there to ask the Lord for forgiveness. While making sacrifices was the right step toward God, genuine repentance requires daily obedience.

The narrative now looks back in time to the days before Joshua passed away. After Joshua gave his farewell charge and dismissed the tribes, the Israelites went out to claim the land God had assigned them. Each family traveled to settle its own inherited property.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars view this verse as the true opening of the main book, which they believe was compiled by later Deuteronomistic editors during the seventh or sixth century BC.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic scholars have generally held that the prophet Samuel authored the book using older tribal records, seeing this section as introducing the spiritual pattern of the judges.

notes.meaning: The Israelites remained faithful to the Lord throughout the lifetime of Joshua and the elders who lived after him. These older leaders had witnessed firsthand the mighty miracles God worked when rescuing and settling His people. Their personal memory of God's power helped anchor the nation in obedience.

Joshua died at the age of one hundred and ten after many decades of guiding Israel. Scripture honors him with the title 'servant of the Lord,' the same title given to Moses. His passing marked the close of a faithful era in Israel's history.

The Israelites buried Joshua on the land given to him at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. Giving him an honorable burial in his own inheritance showed their deep respect for his leadership.

Soon all the people of Joshua's generation passed away and were buried. A new generation grew up that had no firsthand experience of the Lord's mighty deeds in Egypt and the wilderness. Because they did not truly know God for themselves, their faith quickly faded.

The new generation turned away from God and did what was evil in His sight. They began serving the Baals, which were local Canaanite gods regarded as masters or lords over nature. Israel committed this sin openly, right in front of the God who had blessed them.

The Israelites abandoned the Lord, the God who had miraculously freed their ancestors from slavery in Egypt. They chased after the idols of the neighboring nations and bowed down before them. This terrible ingratitude provoked God's righteous anger.

Israel completely cast aside the worship of the Lord and bowed to Baal and the Ashtoreths. Baal was the Canaanite storm god linked with weather and farming, while Ashtoreth was a goddess associated with fertility and warfare. These pagan practices dragged the people into degrading rituals.

God's anger burned against Israel because of their unfaithfulness, so He handed them over to raiders who plundered their homes and crops. He sold them into the hands of surrounding enemies, treating them like property handed over to a buyer. The Israelites could no longer stand firm against their foes.

Whenever the Israelites marched out to war, the Lord's hand was against them to bring defeat rather than victory. This judgment came exactly as God had warned in His law if they broke His covenant. As a result, the nation was thrown into great distress.

Even after Israel rebelled, the Lord had mercy on them and raised up leaders called judges. These judges were not just legal arbiters in courtrooms, but military heroes and rulers inspired by God to deliver the people from foreign oppressors. God used them to rescue the nation from complete destruction.

Israel refused to listen consistently even to the judges God sent. Instead, they acted like an unfaithful spouse, committing spiritual adultery by running after false gods. They quickly abandoned the path of obedience that their ancestors had walked.

Whenever the Lord appointed a judge, He stood by that leader and saved the people from their enemies for as long as the judge lived. God was moved with deep compassion when He heard the groans of His oppressed people. His love answered their misery even when their hearts were unstable.

As soon as the judge died, the people went right back to their old habits and behaved even worse than their ancestors. They worshipped pagan gods and stubbornly refused to give up their corrupt ways. Each cycle plunged the nation into deeper wickedness.

The Lord's anger flared once again because the nation had broken the sacred covenant He gave to their ancestors. Israel repeatedly ignored His voice and followed foreign gods instead. Therefore, God pronounced a solemn judgment upon their rebellion.

God announced that He would no longer drive out any of the nations that Joshua had left unsubdued when he died. Since Israel had chosen to break their promise, the Lord withdrew His supernatural help in warfare. The pagan kingdoms would remain in the land as a consequence of Israel's unfaithfulness.

God used these surviving nations to test whether Israel would choose to obey Him. The test was meant to show the people their own hearts and whether they would follow the Lord like their ancestors did. Temptation reveals whether faith is genuine or shallow.

Because of Israel's disobedience, the Lord left those nations in the land rather than clearing them out quickly. Their continued presence served both as a punishment for sin and as a training ground for the nation's faith. God remained in control of history, even while disciplining His people.
